title: Late-phase type 1 hypersensitivity: eosinophil major basic protein causes the delayed swelling
vignette: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department due to wheezing and difficulty breathing. The patient had been trick-or-treating with his parents and ate several packs of candy containing peanuts. After he receives an intramuscular epinephrine injection, his symptoms resolve. At a follow up appointment, an allergy specialist places droplets of various allergens on the patient's skin and punctures the epidermis at each site. After 15 minutes, the skin at the site with peanut extract is erythematous with a raised, itchy bump that improves by the time the family leaves the office. Three hours later, the parents notice increased swelling at the puncture site. Which of the following is most likely involved in this secondary reaction?

clues.text: ate several packs of candy containing peanuts
clues.note: Peanut is a classic allergen causing IgE-mediated (type I) hypersensitivity, including anaphylaxis (treated with epinephrine).
The immediate wheal-and-flare (within minutes, then fading) is the EARLY phase of type I hypersensitivity: IgE-crosslinked mast cells release histamine -> vasodilation/edema.

clues.text: Three hours later, the parents notice increased swelling at the puncture site
clues.note: A SECOND wave of swelling HOURS later is the LATE phase of type I hypersensitivity: IgE-stimulated Th2/IL-5 recruit EOSINOPHILS, which release MAJOR BASIC PROTEIN causing tissue damage/edema.

whatMatters: The immediate wheal is the EARLY phase (mast cell histamine). The swelling HOURS LATER is the LATE PHASE of type I hypersensitivity: EOSINOPHILS (recruited via Th2/IL-5) release MAJOR BASIC PROTEIN and other cationic proteins that cause tissue damage and the delayed, indurated swelling. Answer C.
strategy: Split type I hypersensitivity into early (minutes: mast cell histamine, wheal-and-flare) and late (hours: eosinophil recruitment, MAJOR BASIC PROTEIN, induration). The delayed swelling is the LATE phase -> eosinophil major basic protein. Reject IgG cell lysis (type II), immune-complex complement (type III), IgE histamine from mast cells (that is the EARLY phase), and CD4 interferon-gamma (type IV, delayed over DAYS not hours).

options.text: Cell lysis following IgG autoantibody binding
Epithelial damage by major basic protein
IgE-mediated histamine release from mast cells
Interferon gamma release from CD4+ T cells

eliminations.label: IgG-mediated cell lysis - type II hypersensitivity
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: IgG binding cell-surface antigens causing complement/NK-mediated lysis (type II). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: type II reactions (e.g., hemolysis) develop over hours-days against cells, not the eosinophil-driven late phase of an IgE allergy. ✅ Correct if: autoimmune hemolysis/cytopenias (type II).

eliminations.label: Immune complex complement - type III hypersensitivity
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: antigen-antibody immune complexes depositing and activating complement (type III). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: an Arthus/serum-sickness reaction differs from the IgE late phase; the delayed swelling here is eosinophil-mediated. ✅ Correct if: immune-complex vasculitis/Arthus reaction.

eliminations.label: IgE histamine from mast cells - the EARLY phase
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: IgE-crosslinked mast cells releasing preformed histamine. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: that mechanism produces the IMMEDIATE wheal-and-flare (minutes), which already faded; the question asks about the LATE (hours-later) swelling. ✅ Correct if: the immediate reaction (early phase).

eliminations.label: CD4 interferon gamma - type IV (days)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: CD4+ T-cell/macrophage-mediated delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: type IV reactions develop over DAYS (e.g., PPD/contact dermatitis) due to cellular amplification; this swelling appeared within HOURS as the IgE late phase. ✅ Correct if: 48-72 hour indurated reaction (TB skin test).

reasoning: Peanut allergy is IgE-mediated (type I) hypersensitivity
The immediate wheal is the early phase (mast cell histamine)
Swelling hours later is the late phase: Th2/IL-5-recruited eosinophils release major basic protein
-> epithelial damage by major basic protein; answer C
mechanism: TYPE I (IMMEDIATE) HYPERSENSITIVITY has two temporal phases. After first exposure, allergen-specific IgE (made by B cells under Th2 help) binds mast cells. On RE-EXPOSURE, allergen CROSS-LINKS IgE on mast cells, triggering degranulation and release of preformed HISTAMINE (and leukotrienes), causing the EARLY-PHASE response within MINUTES: vasodilation and increased capillary permeability producing the WHEAL-AND-FLARE (and, systemically, anaphylaxis - treated with epinephrine). The LATE-PHASE response occurs HOURS later: IgE-activated mast cells and Th2 cells release cytokines (notably IL-5) that recruit and activate EOSINOPHILS. Eosinophils release cationic granule proteins - MAJOR BASIC PROTEIN and eosinophil peroxidase - that cause TISSUE (epithelial) DAMAGE, producing a palpable, indurated swelling 2-10 hours after the early reaction. Therefore the delayed swelling reflects eosinophil MAJOR BASIC PROTEIN. The distractors are other hypersensitivity types: IgG cell lysis (II), immune-complex complement (III), the EARLY-phase mast cell histamine (not late), and CD4 interferon-gamma (type IV, over days).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Immuno > type I hypersensitivity: early phase (mast cell histamine, wheal-and-flare, minutes) and late phase (eosinophils via IL-5, major basic protein, tissue damage, hours later); IgE cross-linking; epinephrine for anaphylaxis.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Immediate wheal = mast cell histamine; swelling hours later = eosinophil major basic protein (late phase).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on type I hypersensitivity, early vs late phase, IgE/mast cells, IL-5/eosinophils, or major basic protein? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: IgG lysis = type II; immune complex = type III; IgE histamine = EARLY phase; CD4 IFN-gamma = type IV (days).

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: type I late phase (hours) = eosinophil major basic protein; early phase (minutes) = mast cell histamine.

keywords.back: Eosinophil major basic protein (recruited by IL-5)

firstAid.detail: Immuno: eosinophil major basic protein -> delayed swelling.
Immuno > mast cell histamine (min) vs eosinophils (hours).
Immuno > II (IgG lysis), III (immune complex), IV (CD4, days).

memoryHook: First a quick histamine welt (minutes), then eosinophils roll in hours later and blast major basic protein - the delayed swelling is the LATE phase of the allergy.
